notes.1ai: Nearly all candidates were able to calculate the concentration of vitamin C in test-tube C . A few candidates incorrectly gave a value of 75% instead of 0.75%. Many candidates find percentage values less than 1% quite challenging. It is also important that values of less than one have a zero before the decimal point, i.e. 0.75 rather than .75.
notes.1aii: Most candidates were able to produce a table of results with a sufficient number of values that followed the correct trend. Candidates should be reminded that units should be included in the table headings and not in the body of the table.
notes.1aiii: Most candidates could state a conclusion for the results they obtained but a few gave answers that were too vague or simply described the results. Answers such as; ‘it goes up with more vitamin C’ are insufficient as both variables need to be included in the conclusion. Similarly, stating that ‘D took 20 drops to become clear’ is a description rather than a conclusion.
notes.1aiv: All candidates were able to give an appropriate answer for the number of drops required for health drink H .
notes.1av: Many candidates were able to estimate a value for health drink H which was in line with their results in 1(a)(ii) . A few used values of 25% to 50% instead of 0.25% to 0.50%.
notes.1avi: Candidates were required to identify two variables that were kept constant. Candidates should be encouraged to avoid the term amount and instead should specify the volume of vitamin C or the concentration of DCPIP, or state the actual volume/concentration that was used.
notes.1avii: Nearly all candidates gave a good description of why the contents of each test-tube were swirled.
notes.1b: Candidates were asked to provide two improvements that would allow for a more accurate estimation of the concentration of vitamin C in health drink H . Many answers were too vague and did not focus on the accuracy of the estimate.
notes.1c: This question was generally well answered with many candidates recognising that the size of the drops could vary.
notes.1d: Candidates were asked to recall the tests for protein and glucose. Many candidates confused biuret and Benedict’s reagents and gave incorrect colours for a positive test result.
notes.2ai: Candidates should be able to produce a biological drawing using a sharp pencil that exhibits clear and continuous lines. It is important that candidates do not use shading. Detail of the leaf shape or venation needs to be recorded accurately.
notes.2aii: Candidates were required to show on their drawing the line at which they took the measurement for leaf length. The majority did this well but a few omitted the line or drew a line that did not coincide with the length of the leaf. All measurements must be in either millimetres or centimetres, inches are not acceptable. Most candidates calculated the magnification correctly although a small number inverted the values in the equation.
notes.2bi: The quality of the graph was very high for many candidates. Some key points to consider when drawing graphs: • Labels on the axes should be complete and include units where appropriate. • Axes do not have to start at zero, but when they do not, this needs to be indicated. • Plotted points must be small, a small cross or circled dot is ideal. • A line of best fit can be a straight line or a curved line, depending on the data. In many cases, joining plotted points with straight lines is sufficient, unless a line of best fit is specifically asked for. • Lines of best fit should not show extrapolation unless specifically asked for in the question.
notes.2bii: When describing a trend both variables need to be mentioned. Simply saying that ‘the lines goes up’ is not specific enough to be credited. A suitable conclusion would state that as the concentration of carbon dioxide increased the number of bubbles produced in five minutes also increased.
notes.2biii: Candidates performed well on this calculation of the rate of photosynthesis. The difference between one significant figure and one decimal place needs to be emphasised to candidates as an answer of 2.8 bubbles per minute was commonly seen.
notes.2biv: Most candidates could identify the independent variable, but many stated amount, instead of being specific and stating concentration.
notes.2c: Some candidates found this question demanding. When writing plans, candidates should remember to: • state the independent variable and explain how this variable is changed, in this case moving a lamp further from the plant • identify the dependent variable and describe how it is to be measured, in this case collecting the volume of gas produced in a set time • identify the factors which need to be kept constant, in this case temperature, pH and concentration of carbon dioxide • state that there needs to be at least two repeats (three trials in total).
